title: The Hidden Economics of Connection
author: Jason L. Zimmerman
summary: Jason Zimmerman opens with a private equity insider's observation that financial engineering has been squeezed dry as a source of returns, pushing sophisticated investors to look at something softer-sounding: the quality of connection between people inside an organization. Zimmerman argues every organization makes an implicit economic bet that 1+1 will equal more than 2, but weak connection between interdependent colleagues doesn't stop work, it just makes it quietly more expensive through duplicated effort, stuck information, and accumulating friction, a claim he backs with a 112-study, nearly-8,000-team meta-analysis showing trust matters most precisely when people with different skills must depend on each other. Using Jody Hoffer Gittell's hospital research and Ronald Burt's study of idea generation among tech-company managers, he distinguishes two different kinds of valuable connection, cohesive relationships that make execution fast and broad network range that exposes people to unfamiliar ideas, arguing organizations need to know which kind their goal actually requires rather than simply pursuing "more connection." His closing argument returns to the private equity room: capital structures, technology, and processes can all be copied by competitors, but the informal relational architecture that determines whether combined human capability becomes more than the sum of its parts cannot be purchased, making connection a genuine, measurable economic asset rather than a soft cultural nicety.
points: The piece's foundational economic claim is precise and countable, not just evocative: weak connection between interdependent workers doesn't halt work, it 'just gets more expensive' through duplicated effort and accumulating friction, so 'the organization may have paid for two units of capability, yet the system produces something closer to 1.7.'

The Reagans and McEvily research supplies a genuine tension leaders must navigate, not just a single lever to pull: cohesive relationships increase people's willingness to share knowledge, while broader, weaker network range increases the ability to transfer knowledge across unfamiliar groups, meaning the two forms of connection trade off against each other rather than simply adding up.

The Steve Jobs/Pixar atrium example is used to make a specific claim about mechanism, not architecture for its own sake: the point of forcing cross-departmental physical proximity 'was not collaboration for collaboration's sake. It was exposure,' directly linking to Ronald Burt's finding that idea quality tracked exposure to disconnected groups, not individual intelligence.

Zimmerman's closing reframe gives leaders a genuine competitive-moat argument for investing in relational architecture: 'capital structures can be copied... technology can be purchased... what is much harder to copy is the system through which all of those things come together,' positioning connection as a durable, non-replicable asset rather than a soft cultural add-on.
quotes: Private equity, he argued, has gotten very good at financial engineering. There was only so much value left to squeeze from changing capital structures, cutting costs, or renegotiating contracts. The next frontier, he suggested, sits inside the organization itself: culture, people, and connection.
The organization may have paid for two units of capability, yet the system produces something closer to 1.7. That is where connection matters.

A large meta-analysis of 112 studies, covering nearly 8,000 teams, found a meaningful relationship between trust and team performance. More interestingly, trust mattered more when the work required people with different skills to depend heavily on one another.

Research by Jody Hoffer Gittell found that stronger relationships built around shared goals, shared knowledge, mutual respect, and timely communication were associated with better patient care and greater operating efficiency, including shorter lengths of stay.

The point was not collaboration for collaboration's sake. It was exposure. Sociologist Ronald Burt studied managers inside a large technology company and found that people who connected otherwise disconnected groups were more likely to develop ideas others judged as valuable.
Capital structures can be copied. Technology can be purchased. Processes can spread quickly across portfolio companies.
